name: Transport points: stops, stations, terminals, airports, taxi stands and chargers
plain: Every mapped point that helps people get around: scheduled bus, train and ferry stops, plus stations, terminals, airports, taxi stands and electric vehicle chargers. The 2026-10 snapshot has 4,405 points, and each one says where it came from.
definition: The file transport.json holds one record per point. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 3,847 records are scheduled stops taken from public timetables in GTFS format (General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, the Integrated Transport Authority) and from 24 municipalities; 544 records are points that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap (OSM): bus stops, bus stations, ferry terminals, airports, taxi stands and electric vehicle (EV) chargers; and 14 records are airports from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) list. The field source tells which group a record belongs to. Only scheduled stops carry routes, modes, weekday stop calls (shown on the map as weekday departures), Saturday and Sunday stop calls (calls_sat and calls_sun), the end date of their timetable feed (feed_end) and the operator_name field. OpenStreetMap points can carry operator text that volunteers typed in the operator field.
unit: points (one record per stop, station, terminal, airport, stand or charger)
geography: Puerto Rico: main island, Vieques and Culebra; each point also carries its municipality

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

method: 1. Scheduled stops: network.py reads every GTFS feed and keeps the boarding points (stops whose location_type is blank or 0) that lie inside Puerto Rico. 2. Mapped points: transport.py asks the Overpass API of OpenStreetMap for bus stops, bus stations, rail and public-transport stations, ferry terminals, taxi stands, bicycle rental, charging stations, aerodromes and helipads inside a box from 17.85 to 18.57 degrees north and 67.97 to 65.20 degrees west. 3. Airports: every airport whose state is PR in the FAA layer of the National Transportation Atlas Database of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. 4. Duplicates (checked only at a full build, which rebuilds all of the observatory's data): an OSM bus stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal within 30 m of a scheduled stop is dropped; an OSM rail station or ferry terminal within 200 m, or bus station within 100 m, of a scheduled or already kept point of the same kind is dropped; an OSM aerodrome within 2 km of an FAA airport is dropped. In the OSM pull of 2026-10-01, 1,804 bus stops, 78 bus stations, 16 rail stations, 13 ferry terminals and 24 aerodromes were mapped; 459, 47, 0, 7 and 11 remain. 5. Each point is given a municipality from its location.
source_detail: ATI GTFS zip (PRITA_GTFS.zip on docs.pr.gov) and the municipal GTFS zips listed in the Transitland Atlas registry of the National Rural Transit Assistance Program (RTAP) portal; OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API; FAA airports from the National Transportation Atlas Database of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics
how_to_read: Look at source first. A point from ati_gtfs or muni_gtfs appears in an operator's published timetable. A point from osm_transport only shows that someone mapped a stop there; it does not show that a vehicle calls there today. A point from faa_airports is an airport record, not a transit stop.
caveats: Stops from expired timetables stay in the file. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 966 of the 3,847 scheduled stops belong to the 7 operators whose feed had ended by the build date (2026-10-02).
Points that volunteers mapped can be missing, out of date or wrong; the observatory does not check them on the ground.
Taxi stands and EV chargers are listed because they help visitors get around. They are not public transit and are not counted as stops.

Licenses differ by source: ATI states its feed is provided without warranty and that an app built on its data must make clear it is not affiliated with or sponsored by ATI; the municipal feeds state no license; OpenStreetMap data is under the Open Database License (ODbL); the FAA list is a US Government source. Check each source's terms before reusing the points.
Duplicates between OpenStreetMap points and scheduled stops are removed only at a full build. The nightly refresh replaces the scheduled stops and does not repeat that check.

Scheduled stops are not merged with each other, so a count of points is a count of records, not of distinct places. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 167 pairs of stops of different operators lie within 30 m of each other (the same physical stop can appear once for ATI and once for a municipal system), and 122 positions hold two stops of the same operator.

The airport kind counts mapped aerodromes, not airports with service. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 11 from OpenStreetMap include two seaplane bases, two fields named Histórico, a military field and a facility whose name says CERRADO (closed), and Fajardo's Aeropuerto Diego Jiménez Torres comes only from OpenStreetMap.

name: Scheduled versus mapped transit points
plain: A scheduled stop is in a timetable that an operator published; a mapped stop is a point that volunteers drew in OpenStreetMap. Only scheduled stops come with routes, weekday departures and the operator_name field; mapped points can carry operator text that volunteers typed.
definition: Scheduled: a boarding point in the stops file of a public timetable feed in GTFS format (General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or from a municipality; the source is ati_gtfs or muni_gtfs. The same feed says which routes call at the stop and at what times, so the observatory can count weekday departures. Mapped: a point or area tagged in OpenStreetMap as a bus stop, station, terminal, taxi stand, charger or airport (source osm_transport). The tag says the object exists; it holds no timetable. Airports from the list of the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration; source faa_airports) are a third group: a federal register of airports, not a transit timetable.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

method: Scheduled stops come from network.py. Mapped points come from transport.py. A mapped bus stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal that lies next to a scheduled one is dropped and the scheduled record wins (distances are in the entry on distance rules). This check runs only at a full build. Scheduled stops are not merged with each other: the same physical stop can appear once for Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and once for a municipal system, and one operator can list two stops at the same position.
how_to_read: Tools that need a timetable use scheduled stops only: service coverage (residents within 400 m), service gaps, integration points, route counts and the replay of vehicles on their timetable. Tools that only need to know where a stop physically is use scheduled and mapped stops together: the 400 m walk rings on the map and the share of tourism places within 400 m of any mapped stop (kinds transit_stop, bus_stop, bus_station, rail_station and ferry_terminal). The access of tourism places to a stop with a current timetable (place_access.json and the acc_ fields of municipalities.json) uses scheduled stops only, and only those whose operator's feed has not ended.
caveats: A scheduled stop from an expired timetable is not proof of service today, and a mapped stop is not proof of service at all.
How complete the mapped stops are depends on volunteer mapping. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 393 of the 459 mapped bus stops name the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses as operator.
A count of stops is a count of records, not of distinct places. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 167 pairs of scheduled stops of different operators lie within 30 m of each other.

name: Transport point id
plain: A unique text id for each transport point. It starts with where the point came from.
definition: Text id, unique in transport.json. Scheduled stops: gtfs, then the operator id, then the stop id used in that operator's feed (example gtfs:ati:1017). OpenStreetMap (OSM) points: osm: followed by n for a node or w for a way, then the OpenStreetMap number (example osm:n368381564). Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airports: faa: followed by the FAA location id (example faa:SJU). The examples are from the 2026-10 snapshot.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

method: Built by network.py (scheduled stops), transport.py (OSM points) and the FAA loader in transport.py.
source_detail: GTFS stops.txt field stop_id (prefixed gtfs:<operator>:); OpenStreetMap element type (n for node, w for way) and number; FAA location id (loc_id)
how_to_read: Use the id to point to one record in this snapshot.
caveats: A scheduled stop's id contains the feed's own stop id, so it changes if the operator renumbers its stops. Do not use it to follow a stop over time.
Some feed stop ids contain spaces or capital letters. In the 2026-10 snapshot, an example is the Vieques stop gtfs:vieques:EL GALLITO BEACH.

name: Transport point name
plain: The name of the stop, station, terminal, airport, stand or charger, as its source gives it. A few names are blank, misspelled or missing letters in the source.
definition: Scheduled stops: the stop_name in the operator's feed, trimmed. OpenStreetMap (OSM) points: the name tag, otherwise the ref tag, otherwise empty text. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airports: the facility name, converted from capitals to title case. Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) names usually describe a position on a street (for example a road and the cross street it is next to) rather than a place name.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

method: Copied from the source without correction.
source_detail: GTFS stops.txt field stop_name; OpenStreetMap tags name, then ref; FAA Aviation Facilities layer 0 of the National Transportation Atlas Database, field fac_name
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 48 OSM points have no name (the value is empty text).

Some municipal feeds have lost accented letters in the source file itself (in the 2026-10 snapshot, for example, Pblicos for Públicos and Estacin for Estación), and some lose a letter inside a word (for example Funeraria Marn for Marín). The observatory does not repair them.
FAA names have no accents and may be shortened (in the 2026-10 snapshot, for example, Luis Munoz Marin Intl).

name: Transport point kind
plain: What kind of place the point is: a stop, a bus station, a train station, a ferry terminal, an airport, a taxi stand or a charger.
definition: A code for the type of point. For scheduled stops, which come from the timetables of Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and of municipalities, the kind comes from the feed: a stop served by a rail route is rail_station; one served by a ferry route is ferry_terminal; one whose name starts with Terminal or Estación (and that no rail or ferry route serves) is bus_station; every other scheduled stop is transit_stop. For OpenStreetMap (OSM) points the kind comes from the tags, checked in this order: railway=station (or public_transport=station on an object that also has a railway tag) gives rail_station; amenity=ferry_terminal gives ferry_terminal; amenity=bus_station, or public_transport=station when the point has no railway tag, gives bus_station (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 2 of the 47 mapped bus stations carry only the second tag); highway=bus_stop gives bus_stop; aeroway=aerodrome gives airport; amenity=taxi gives taxi; amenity=charging_station gives ev_charging. The code can also write helipad (aeroway=helipad) and bike_rental (amenity=bicycle_rental) for OSM points; the 2026-10 snapshot has none.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

method: Rules in network.py (parse_gtfs) and transport.py (osm_kind). The kind decides which map layer shows the point: stops layer (transit_stop, bus_stop), stations layer (bus_station, rail_station, ferry_terminal, airport) and taxi layer (taxi, ev_charging, bike_rental, helipad).
source_detail: GTFS routes.txt field route_type (through trips.txt and stop_times.txt) and stops.txt field stop_name; OpenStreetMap tags railway, public_transport, amenity, highway and aeroway
how_to_read: Kind says what the point is, not whether it is scheduled. Combine it with source.
caveats: A scheduled stop is called a bus_station only when its name starts with Terminal or Estación. A terminal with a different name stays transit_stop.
The map popup labels every transit_stop as “Transit stop (ATI)”, although in the 2026-10 snapshot 2,381 of the 3,781 come from municipal feeds. Use the source field to tell them apart.
The rail_station label on the map reads Tren Urbano station. In the 2026-10 snapshot the only rail route is Tren Urbano.

The airport kind counts mapped aerodromes, not airports with service. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 11 from OpenStreetMap include two seaplane bases, two fields named Histórico, a military field and a facility whose name says CERRADO (closed), and Fajardo's Aeropuerto Diego Jiménez Torres comes only from OpenStreetMap.

name: Transport point location (latitude and longitude)
plain: Where the point is, as latitude and longitude in decimal degrees.
definition: Latitude (lat, degrees north) and longitude (lng, degrees east, so negative in Puerto Rico) in the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS 84), the reference system used by satellite navigation. Scheduled stops: the feed's coordinates rounded to 5 decimals (about 1 m). OpenStreetMap (OSM) points: 6 decimals; for areas such as a station building, the centre point. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airports: the position in the FAA layer, 6 decimals. In the 2026-10 snapshot, latitudes run from 17.965554 to 18.507643 and longitudes from -67.931886 to -65.30252.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

method: Scheduled stops: if a feed gives a positive longitude between 65 and 68 (the minus sign was lost, as in Jayuya's feed in the 2026-10 snapshot), the observatory changes its sign. A stop outside latitude 17.5 to 18.8 and longitude -68 to -65 is dropped.
source_detail: GTFS stops.txt fields stop_lat and stop_lon; OpenStreetMap node position or way centre; FAA Aviation Facilities layer 0 of the National Transportation Atlas Database, point geometry
caveats: Positions are as precise as the source. A scheduled stop can sit some metres from the real pole or shelter.
The sign correction is a rule on the longitude only; it does not test whether the stop is on a road.

name: Scheduled weekday calls at the stop (shown on the map as weekday departures)
plain: How many times the published timetable has a vehicle call at the stop on a typical weekday. The map popup calls it weekday departures.
definition: Number of stop times at this stop (a stop time is one line in a feed saying that a trip calls at a stop at a given time), counting every trip in the feed whose service runs on the reference weekday (Wednesday, or the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that the feed serves). A trip that calls at the stop twice counts twice. It counts every scheduled call, including the last stop of a trip, where the vehicle ends its run. Only scheduled stops have it.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.py counts rows of stop_times.txt per stop for trips on the weekday service. It does not apply the feed's calendar_dates.txt exceptions such as holidays; see Typical weekday.
source_detail: GTFS stop_times.txt, trips.txt and calendar.txt
how_to_read: A higher number means more scheduled calls. In the 2026-10 snapshot the largest is Terminal Covadonga with 508 calls. It does not tell how full vehicles are or whether they run on time. A timetable covers the dates from the operator's feed.start to feed.end in operators.json, not the build date. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31; Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31. Cite both the build date and the feed dates.
caveats: It counts calls in the timetable, not vehicles seen.

The Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed read on 2026-10-02 includes 30 trips on a holiday service pattern that is counted as ordinary weekday service (see Typical weekday), so stops on ATI route 1 are slightly overstated.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, one scheduled stop has 0 because no trip calls there.
At a terminal the count includes vehicles that arrive and stop there, not only vehicles that leave.

The stop popup on the map shows this number as weekday departures even when the operator's timetable has ended. The popup also shows the end date of the timetable (feed_end) and says 'Timetable ended' when that date has passed.
The same field name, trips_weekday, counts trips on a route in transit_routes.geojson and operators.json. Here it counts stop calls, so the values are not comparable.

name: Scheduled Saturday calls at the stop (shown on the map as Saturday departures)
plain: How many times the published timetable has a vehicle call at the stop on a typical Saturday. The map popup shows it as Saturday departures. The field is missing when the feed lists no Saturday call at the stop.
definition: Number of stop times at this stop (a stop time is one line in a feed saying that a trip calls at a stop at a given time) for trips whose service pattern runs on Saturday (saturday = 1 in the feed's calendar.txt). A trip that calls at the stop twice counts twice, and every call counts, including the last stop of a trip. The field is left out when the count is 0, so a missing field means that the feed lists no Saturday call at this stop. Only scheduled stops can have it. In the 2026-10 snapshot 1,910 of the 3,847 scheduled stops have it, with at most 276 calls (Terminal Covadonga).

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: parse_gtfs in network.py counts the rows of stop_times.txt for each stop, on trips whose service pattern runs on Saturday, in the same pass that counts the weekday calls. Like the weekday count, it does not apply the exceptions in calendar_dates.txt (holidays, added or removed dates) and does not check the dates when a pattern starts and ends; see Typical weekday.
source_detail: GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) stop_times.txt, trips.txt and calendar.txt
how_to_read: A higher number means more scheduled Saturday calls. A missing field means that the timetable lists no Saturday call at the stop. It does not prove that no vehicle runs. name: How route lines are drawn
plain: A route line is the operator's own shape when the feed has one, otherwise a path along roads between the stops. If the stop order looks wrong the observatory infers one, and if nothing works it joins the stops with straight dotted lines.
definition: The counts below are for the 2026-10 snapshot. 1. Feed shape: if the feed lists a route shape (the line the operator publishes for the path of a route), the observatory keeps up to the two most used shapes of the route (usually one per direction). 50 routes are drawn this way, including every Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) route. 2. Road-snapped: with no shape, the observatory takes the stops of the longest trip in each direction and links each pair of neighbouring stops by the fastest road path in the OpenStreetMap road network (roads.bin). 94 routes are drawn this way. 3. Inferred order: if a feed lists its stops out of travel order, the observatory picks a plausible order and then snaps it to roads. 5 routes are drawn this way, all from Patillas. 4. Straight dotted: if too little of a route can be snapped, the stops are joined by straight lines and drawn dotted. No route uses this in the 2026-10 snapshot. 5. OpenStreetMap: the 16 públicos and trolley routes are drawn from the lines volunteers mapped.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Road snapping: each stop is moved to the nearest road within 500 m; a leg is accepted if the road path is no longer than 3 times the straight distance plus 400 m; stops less than 25 m apart are joined directly. A route is kept as road-snapped only if at least 60% of the legs in each direction follow a road; otherwise it falls back to straight lines. The line is then simplified (tolerance about 3 m). Inferred order: a feed is flagged when the stop order has a zig-zag ratio above 2.5 (the length of the path through the stops in listed order divided by the length of a nearest-neighbour tour; real routes sit near 1 to 2) or when the stop names are in alphabetical order. The order is then rebuilt from the terminal or first stop by always going to the nearest unvisited stop by road, improved by reversing stretches of the order while that shortens the road distance, and the line returns to its start; for more than 45 distinct stops the order is not rebuilt and the route falls back to straight lines. A route whose stops did not change keeps its previous line (see the entry on the route line fingerprint).
how_to_read: On the map a solid line follows the operator's shape or the roads, a lighter dashed line is a route with inferred stop order, a dotted line joins stops straight, and a gold dashed line is an OpenStreetMap route. Ferries are dashed teal.
caveats: Only a feed shape is the operator's own alignment. A road-snapped line is an estimate and the real street may differ.
A route with an inferred order shows a plausible path, not the route the operator runs. Its times are left out of the timetable replay.
The feed's route colour is not used on the map; line colour follows the mode and the type of operator.
Road-snapped lines are derived from OpenStreetMap roads, which are under the Open Database License. Credit OpenStreetMap contributors and check the license terms before reuse.

definition: The route_short_name in the feed, or the OpenStreetMap (OSM) ref tag. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is empty text for 57 of 165 routes; Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) routes all have one.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Copied from the source.

caveats: A short name is only unique within an operator.

name: Transit route name
plain: The route's full name, usually the places it connects, such as Ceiba-Mosquitos (example from the 2026-10 snapshot).
definition: The route_long_name in the feed. For OpenStreetMap (OSM) routes: the name tag, else the description, else the network or operator tag, else Unnamed route. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is empty text for 18 of 165 routes (Caguas, San Lorenzo and Vieques leave it empty).

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Copied from the source.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: ROUTE_TYPES in network.py.
source_detail: GTFS routes.txt field route_type; always bus for OpenStreetMap routes
caveats: The codes tram, cable, gondola and funicular are possible but not present in the 2026-10 snapshot.

values.ferry: Ferry route (AcuaExpreso). 4 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.rail: Rail route (Tren Urbano). 1 route in the 2026-10 snapshot.

Tram, cable, gondola and funicular are not present in the 2026-10 snapshot. OpenStreetMap (OSM) routes: Público if the OSM route type is share_taxi or the network name contains público, otherwise Bus.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

name: Transit route colour in the feed
plain: The colour the operator gave the route in its feed, as a hex code such as #0000FF. The map does not use it.
definition: The route_color of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) or municipal feed written as # and six hex digits, when the feed gives a valid one. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is present on 113 routes (67 different colours) and null for the other 52, including every OpenStreetMap (OSM) route.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Copied from the feed after checking that it has exactly six hex digits.
source_detail: GTFS routes.txt field route_color
how_to_read: Use it only if you want the operator's own colour scheme.
caveats: The map and the 3D view colour lines by mode and type of operator and ignore this field: rail red, ferries teal, ATI buses blue, municipal buses green and OSM routes gold.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

name: Scheduled trips per day on the route
plain: How many trips the operator's timetable has on this route on a typical weekday, a Saturday and a Sunday. Zero means none listed, which for volunteer-mapped routes means no timetable.
definition: Three counts per route: trips_weekday, trips_saturday and trips_sunday. A trip is one scheduled run listed in the feed's trips file (a feed is the set of GTFS files in which an operator publishes its stops, routes, trips and times). Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and Guaynabo list each direction as its own trip, so an out-and-back journey counts as two. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the other 23 feeds give every trip of a route the same direction code, so a trip there may be one leg or a whole loop. The weekday count uses the reference weekday described under Typical weekday. In the 2026-10 snapshot the largest values are 166 on weekdays and 138 on Saturdays and Sundays (Tren Urbano).

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.py counts the trips of the route whose service runs on each day type. Exceptions in calendar_dates.txt (holidays, added or removed dates) are not applied, and the date range of each service pattern is not checked.
source_detail: GTFS trips.txt joined to calendar.txt (service days); calendar_dates.txt only when a feed has no calendar.txt
how_to_read: Compare routes of the same operator. A route with more trips has more scheduled service. The map draws wider lines for higher weekday counts. A timetable covers the dates from the operator's feed.start to feed.end in operators.json, not the build date. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31; Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31. Cite both the build date and the feed dates.
caveats: In the ATI feed read on 2026-10-02, route 1 shows 81 weekday trips, but 30 of them belong to a holiday service pattern that the feed removes on most dates. Without them the count is 51.
A feed that gives no Saturday or Sunday service shows 0 for those days. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only ATI, Guaynabo, Juncos and Vega Alta list Saturday service, and only ATI lists Sunday service.
Counts are for the timetable in the feed, whether or not it has expired.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

name: First and last weekday departure on the route
plain: The earliest and the latest time a weekday trip on the route starts, in seconds after midnight. The map shows them as clock times.
definition: first is the earliest and last is the latest departure from the first stop of any weekday trip on the route. Seconds after midnight, local time (12600 is 03:30). In the 2026-10 snapshot it is present for 149 routes; first runs from 12600 (03:30) to 29700 (08:15) and last from 39600 (11:00) to 84600 (23:30). It is null for the 16 OpenStreetMap (OSM) routes.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.py sorts the time at the first stop of each weekday trip and keeps the smallest and the largest.
source_detail: GTFS stop_times.txt (time at the first stop of each weekday trip), joined to trips.txt and calendar.txt
how_to_read: Divide by 3600 to get hours. last is when the final trip leaves its first stop, not when it arrives. A timetable covers the dates from the operator's feed.start to feed.end in operators.json, not the build date. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31; Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31. Cite both the build date and the feed dates.
caveats: For Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and Guaynabo, which list each direction, the two values mix both directions of travel; in the 2026-10 snapshot the other 23 feeds do not separate directions.
They are taken from the stop times as listed, so in the 2026-10 snapshot the five Patillas routes with an inferred stop order also show them even though their times are not used in the replay.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

name: How the route line was drawn
plain: Says whether the line is the operator's own shape, a path along roads, a path along roads with a guessed stop order, or a volunteer-mapped line.
definition: A code for how the line of a route from Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), a municipality or OpenStreetMap was made. The code stops (a straight dotted line joining the stops) exists in the program but no route uses it in the 2026-10 snapshot.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Set by network.py (shape, stops), snap_routes (roads, roads_inferred) and load_osm_routes (osm). See How route lines are drawn.
source_detail: GTFS shapes.txt (shape); the OpenStreetMap road network, Geofabrik Puerto Rico extract (roads.bin), for roads and roads_inferred; OpenStreetMap route relations (osm)
how_to_read: Trust shape most. Treat roads as a good estimate, roads_inferred as a rough guess, and osm as a volunteer map.
caveats: The code stops would appear as a dotted straight line; none is present in the 2026-10 snapshot.

values.shape: The route shape published in the feed. 50 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot (all ATI routes and 12 municipal ones).
values.roads: No shape in the feed; the line follows roads between the stops in listed order. 94 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.roads_inferred: The feed lists the stops out of travel order, so the order of visit is inferred and the line follows roads. 5 routes (Patillas) in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.osm: Line mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap. 16 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

name: Route line fingerprint
plain: A short technical code used to decide whether a road-snapped line must be redrawn. It has no meaning for readers.
definition: The first 12 hexadecimal digits of an MD5 checksum (a fixed-length fingerprint of text) of the route's stop sequence plus the version of the snapping method. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is present on the 99 routes drawn along roads, all of them municipal routes, and absent on shape and OpenStreetMap (OSM) routes.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: snap_routes in network.py. If a route's sig matches the one in the last published file, the earlier line is reused instead of snapping again.
source_detail: Computed by network.py from the stop sequence of the route (GTFS stop_times.txt and stops.txt)
how_to_read: Ignore it for analysis. A changed sig means the stops of the route or the snapping method changed.
caveats: It is not an identifier. Use operator and route_id to point to a route.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

name: Note on a feed's stop order
plain: A sentence that explains why the observatory had to guess the order of a route's stops. In the 2026-10 snapshot it appears on five Patillas routes.
definition: Text, present only on routes whose feed lists the stops out of travel order. It states the zig-zag ratio found and that the order of visit is inferred and the times are not usable. The sentence says alphabetically when the stop names are in alphabetical order, and out of travel order otherwise. In the 2026-10 snapshot the five notes give the ratios 2.72, 2.77, 2.93, 4.44 and 4.99, and all five say out of travel order.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Written by snap_routes in network.py when order_quality flags a route (zig-zag ratio above 2.5, or at least 5 stops in alphabetical order).
source_detail: Computed by network.py from the stop order in GTFS stop_times.txt and the stop names in stops.txt
how_to_read: When a note is present, read the line as a plausible path, not the real route.
caveats: Trip counts and first and last times for these routes are still in the file. Their times are left out of the timetable replay files.

name: Network name (OpenStreetMap routes)
plain: The name of the network or operator that volunteers wrote on an OpenStreetMap (OSM) route, such as Carros Públicos. Only OSM routes can have it.
definition: Text of the OSM network tag, or the operator tag when there is no network. The key is present only on OSM routes: in the 2026-10 snapshot on all 16, with a null value on 4 of them. It is absent from feed routes.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Copied from the OSM tags by load_osm_routes.
source_detail: OpenStreetMap route relation tags network, then operator
caveats: The text is free and unchecked. It is not an official operator name.

values.Carros Públicos: 9 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot, all labelled Público.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

name: Operators file: operators, feeds, live checks, coverage and integration points
plain: One file with the list of operators and the state of their timetables, a check of real-time data, residents near stops in each municipality, and places where stops of two systems are close.
definition: The file operators.json is one JSON object with six keys, listed under Codes. A feed is the set of files, in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format, in which one operator publishes its stops, routes, trips and times. The parts of the file have their own entries: the operator record, real-time data, residents counted for coverage and integration points.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Written by network.py and build.py, and rewritten every night by refresh_network.py. Operators with no feed (status none) come last; among the others the regional operator, Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), comes first and the rest follow by short name.
source_detail: FTA National Transit Database 2023 GTFS weblinks table (2023-gtfs-weblinks.csv, report year 2023), read through the Transitland Atlas copy on GitHub; Transitland Atlas registry file feeds/nationalrtap.org.dmfr.json for the National RTAP portal feeds; ATI file PRITA_GTFS.zip
how_to_read: Start with the operator record for the state of each feed, then the coverage records for residents near stops.
caveats: The status stored in the file is the one worked out on the build date. The map recomputes it from the feed end date each time the page opens.
The files do not record when each feed was last downloaded. If a download fails, the previous copy of that feed is kept, so the build date does not prove that every feed was refreshed that night.

Terms differ by source. The terms of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) say the data are provided as is, without warranty, and that an app built on them must make clear it is not affiliated with or sponsored by ATI. The municipal feeds state no license; ask the municipality before reusing a feed beyond viewing it. Parts drawn from OpenStreetMap are under the Open Database License (credit and share-alike). Check each source's terms before reuse.
An operator record can have feed.url set to null when its feed address is not a public web page, and an operator with no feed may have no address at all (see Transit operator record).

values.built: The build date (2026-10-02 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
values.operators: A list of operator records (see Transit operator record): 44 in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.live: An object with checked (the date real-time sources were checked: 2026-10-02 in the 2026-10 snapshot) and sources (a list of checks, 6 in the 2026-10 snapshot; see Real-time vehicle data).
values.coverage: An object with one record for each of the 78 municipalities, keyed by municipality name (for example Vega Baja). Each record holds the residents counted and the residents within 400 m of scheduled stops (see Residents counted for coverage).
values.transfers: A list of pairs of nearby stops of different operators (366 in the 2026-10 snapshot; see Integration points).
values.transfers_total: The number of pairs found before the list is cut at 600 (366 in the 2026-10 snapshot, so all are present).

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Operators list

name: How the operator list is made
plain: The observatory starts from the federal list of transit agencies that report to the National Transit Database, then looks for each agency's public timetable feed. In the 2026-10 snapshot it lists 44 operators and says which ones publish a feed.
definition: 1. Checklist: the 2023 table of General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) web links of the National Transit Database (NTD, run by the Federal Transit Administration), read through the Transitland Atlas copy on GitHub. An agency is kept when its name matches a municipality (a municipal operator), contains Metropolitan Bus Authority (AMA), Highway and Transportation Authority or Público (públicos), or Maritime Transport (the ferry authority). Other agencies are skipped, and a City of San Juan in Texas is skipped by its NTD id. 2. Feeds: the Atlas registry of the National Rural Transit Assistance Program (RTAP) portal is read for municipal static GTFS feed URLs; the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed comes from its open data page. 3. Volunteer routes: OpenStreetMap routes are added as a separate operator. 4. An operator on the checklist with no feed gets status none (or in_ati for AMA and the ferry authority, whose services are in the ATI feed).

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.discover reads both lists whenever a refresh is requested (the nightly refresh always requests one) and otherwise uses its saved copy; if the lists cannot be reached it falls back to the saved copy. A municipality that uploads a feed to the registry appears at the next refresh.
source_detail: FTA National Transit Database 2023 GTFS weblinks table (2023-gtfs-weblinks.csv, report year 2023), read through the Transitland Atlas copy on GitHub; Transitland Atlas registry file feeds/nationalrtap.org.dmfr.json for the National RTAP portal feeds; ATI file PRITA_GTFS.zip
how_to_read: The list is the federal checklist plus ATI, the feeds found and the OpenStreetMap routes. It is not a census of every vehicle service on the island.
caveats: A private público or a bus service that neither reports to the NTD nor publishes a feed is not listed.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Cabo Rojo, Canóvanas and Corozal publish feeds but are not on the NTD checklist, so their records have a null municipality and a null ntd_id. For these three, the municipality fields muni_system and muni_system_routes in municipalities.json therefore read null and 0, even though they publish feeds.
The checklist is the report-year 2023 table, so agencies that started or stopped reporting later are not reflected.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Operators list

name: Transit operator record
plain: One record per operator: its name, type, how many routes, stops and weekday trips it has, and the state of its public timetable feed.
definition: Each record in the operators list describes one operator (44 records in the 2026-10 snapshot). Its keys are listed under Codes. For an operator with no feed, routes, stops and trips_weekday are 0 and modes is an empty list.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Built by build_network in network.py.
how_to_read: Filter on feed.status to see who has current data. Use routes, stops and trips_weekday to compare the size of systems.
caveats: feed.url is the address the timetable file was downloaded from: the ATI file, or a file uploaded to the National Rural Transit Assistance Program (RTAP) portal. It can be null: the observatory leaves it blank when the address is not a public web page.

feed.url is also null for an operator with no feed of its own when the federal list gives no link; where the list gives one, the observatory copies it without checking it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 1 of the 18 operators without a feed of their own has a link (a web page, not a timetable file) and the other 17 are null. For the OpenStreetMap routes the url is the OpenStreetMap home page, not a timetable.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 5 operators have no ntd_id: ATI, the OpenStreetMap routes and three municipal operators that are not on the federal list.
Operator-level trips_weekday counts trips with at least two stop times; the route-level count counts all trips of the route. They are equal in the 2026-10 snapshot.

values.id: Operator id: ati, osm, or a lower-case slug of the municipality or agency name (for example san_juan).
values.name: Full name of the operator.
values.short: Short name for display: ATI for the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, AMA for the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses, OpenStreetMap for the volunteer routes, the municipality's name (for example Bayamón) for a municipal operator, and the full name when no municipality is known (for example Municipality of Cabo Rojo).
values.type: Kind of operator: regional, municipal, ama, ferry, publico or community (see Operator type).
values.municipality: Municipality of a municipal operator on the federal list, else null (in the 2026-10 snapshot also null for the 3 municipal operators that are not on that list).
values.ntd_id: National Transit Database id (a number), or null (5 operators in the 2026-10 snapshot).
values.modes: List of the modes of the routes it publishes (an empty list for operators with no routes).
values.trips_weekday: Weekday trips that have at least two stop times.
values.feed: Object with status, url (the address the timetable was downloaded from; it can be null, see Cautions) and, for operators with a feed, agency, version, start, end, has_shapes, weekend_service and sometimes order_issue (see the feed entries).

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Operators list

name: Transit operator type
plain: Says what kind of operator a record is. There are six kinds: regional (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, ATI), municipal, bus authority (Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses, AMA), ferry, público and community (OpenStreetMap volunteers).
definition: A code for the type of operator, set from its name on the federal checklist or fixed by the observatory (ATI is regional, OpenStreetMap is community). A feed operator that is not on the checklist is recorded as municipal.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.discover and build_network.
source_detail: FTA National Transit Database 2023 GTFS weblinks table (2023-gtfs-weblinks.csv, report year 2023), read through the Transitland Atlas copy on GitHub; Transitland Atlas registry file feeds/nationalrtap.org.dmfr.json; ATI file PRITA_GTFS.zip
caveats: The type says how the operator is listed, not who drives the vehicles.

values.municipal: A municipal agency. In the 2026-10 snapshot there are 39: 36 appear on the federal transit list, and 3 (Cabo Rojo, Canóvanas and Corozal) are known only because they publish a timetable feed; 24 of the 39 have a feed. The observatory does not record whether a municipality runs fixed routes or on-demand service.
values.regional: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), the regional authority (Tren Urbano, Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA) and Metrobús buses, ferries).
values.ama: The Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA), the Metropolitan Bus Authority. Its buses are in the ATI feed, so it has no feed of its own.
values.ferry: Puerto Rico Maritime Transport Authority. Its ferries are in the ATI feed.
values.publico: Puerto Rico Highway and Transportation Authority, Público: the públicos (shared cars and vans). It publishes no timetable feed.

name: Timetable feed status
plain: Says whether an operator's published timetable is still in force: current (more than 60 days left), expiring (60 days or fewer) or expired (the end date has passed). It does not say whether the service runs.
definition: The state of an operator's public timetable, worked out from the feed's end date (feed.end). Expired: the end date is before today. Expiring: the end date is today or up to 60 days ahead. Current: the end date is more than 60 days ahead. Other values apply to operators without a feed or with special cases (for example in_ati: the operator's services are inside the feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, ATI). The stored status uses the build date; the map recomputes it from the Puerto Rico calendar date each time the page opens, so a page opened later never shows current for a feed that has ended.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: feed_status in network.py (build time) and opStatus in network.js (page open). Text on the map: Current, Expires soon, Expired, No public feed, In the ATI feed, Community-mapped.
how_to_read: Use current for planning only after checking the end date. Treat expired timetables as history.
caveats: Expired means the published file ended. The operator may still run service; the public file may simply not have been updated.
Current means the published timetable has not ended. It does not mean vehicles run on time or at all.
The code broken (the feed could not be read; map label Feed error) and unknown (no end date; map label Dates unknown) exist in the program but are not present in the 2026-10 snapshot.

Stops and routes of expired operators stay in the other files. Their lines and stops look the same as current ones on the map; the Expired badge appears only when a route is opened and in the Operators list, and a stop's popup gives the end date of its timetable. The observatory leaves them out of the vehicles-on-their-timetable layer, out of the active coverage figures and out of the access fields of tourism places that need a current timetable.
The feed object also holds url, the address the timetable was downloaded from. It can be null (see Transit operator record).

values.current: The feed's end date is more than 60 days away. 17 operators on 2026-10-02.
values.expiring: The feed ends within 60 days (map label: Expires soon). 1 operator on 2026-10-02.
values.expired: The feed's end date has passed. 7 operators on 2026-10-02.
values.none: The operator is on the federal checklist, but no timetable feed was found in the registry the observatory reads. It may publish elsewhere. 16 operators on 2026-10-02.
values.in_ati: The operator's services are inside the ATI feed (the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses, AMA, and the Maritime Transport Authority ferries). 2 operators on 2026-10-02.
values.community: Routes mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap; there is no timetable. 1 operator on 2026-10-02.

name: Timetable feed dates, version and agency
plain: The first and last date covered by an operator's published timetable, the feed's version label and the agency name written inside the feed.
definition: A feed is the set of files, in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format, in which one operator publishes its stops, routes, trips and times. feed.start and feed.end: the earliest start date and the latest end date among the feed's service patterns (calendar.txt); if the feed has no calendar, the dates in feed_info.txt. Written as YYYY-MM-DD. feed.version: the feed_version text (null for 2 feeds in the 2026-10 snapshot). feed.agency: the first agency name in the feed. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: parse_gtfs in network.py. An operator without a feed has none of these keys.
how_to_read: feed.end is the date after which the published timetable no longer applies.
caveats: start and end come from the whole feed. A single route's own service can end earlier.
The end date is what the publisher entered. In the build of 2026-10-02, Bayamón and Jayuya end on 2029-12-31, far later than the other feeds.
The agency name is the one in the feed and can differ from the operator name (for example Sistema Integrado de Transportación del Sur for Ponce).
The files do not record when each feed was last downloaded. If a download fails, the previous copy of that feed is kept, so the build date does not prove that every feed was refreshed that night.
The feed object also holds url, the address the timetable was downloaded from. It can be null (see Transit operator record).

name: Timetable feed flags: shapes, weekend service and order issues
plain: Three details about a feed: whether it has route shapes, whether it lists weekend service, and how many of its routes list stops out of order.
definition: feed.has_shapes: true when at least one route is drawn from a shape in the feed (6 of 25 feeds in the 2026-10 snapshot). feed.weekend_service: true when any route has Saturday or Sunday trips; in the 2026-10 snapshot this holds for 4 feeds: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), Guaynabo, Juncos and Vega Alta. feed.order_issue: the number of the operator's routes with an out-of-order stop list; the key exists only when it is above 0 (in the 2026-10 snapshot, Patillas, 5).

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: parse_gtfs and build_network in network.py. The OpenStreetMap (OSM) operator has has_shapes true and no weekend_service.
how_to_read: has_shapes false means the operator's lines on the map are drawn along roads by the observatory.
caveats: weekend_service false means the feed lists no Saturday or Sunday trips. Service may exist without being published.

values.true: The condition holds for the feed.
values.false: The condition does not hold, or the feed does not say.

name: Real-time vehicle data: what exists and what does not
plain: On 2 October 2026 no public real-time feed of bus, train or ferry positions was found for Puerto Rico, so the data hold no live vehicle positions. This entry lists what was checked and what each source needs.
definition: The key live in operators.json holds checked (the check date, 2026-10-02) and sources (the list of checks, 6 on that date). Each check has id, name, status, detail and, when there is one, url. The checks of 2026-10-02 cover the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) real-time feed (listed by ATI as in development, with no feed address), the AMA Móvil app (AMA is the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses; positions shown in an app, no public data), ATI express buses (a third-party app says it uses positions the operator publishes; no public feed), municipal systems (none found), the AcuaExpreso ferries (an app, no public feed) and aircraft near Puerto Rico (community data in ADS-B format, Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast, that need a relay).

coverage.frequency: Checked by a person and recorded in the program code (network.py); the program does not re-check the sources. Last checked 2026-10-02

method: The result of each check is written into LIVE_SOURCES in network.py (checked 2026-10-02). The observatory does not test the sources automatically.
source_detail: operators.json key live: live.checked (2026-10-02) and live.sources (6 items with id, name, status, detail and url). Pages checked: ATI open data page, AMA Móvil (AMATrack) on Google Play, transPRte on the Apple App Store, ATI urban transportation page, community ADS-B networks
how_to_read: Where the observatory shows vehicles moving, it is replaying a timetable. See Vehicles on their timetable now.
caveats: The check is a snapshot. A feed published after the check date will not be known until someone updates the list.
The statuses describe public data. An operator can have private tracking that is not shared.

values.not published: The operator has announced the feed but no address exists. Example: the ATI real-time feed, which ATI lists as en desarrollo (in development).
values.app only: Positions are shown in a mobile app, and no public data feed sits behind it (AMA Móvil, the ferries).
values.private feed: A third-party app says it shows positions that the operator publishes. No public feed address exists, and access is said to require a request to ATI (the ATI express buses).
values.none found: No real-time feed exists in the public registries (municipal systems).
values.available, needs a relay: Free live data exist but their servers do not allow calls from a web page, so a small relay service is needed (aircraft, ADS-B).

name: Residents counted for coverage (by municipality)
plain: How many residents each municipality has in the coverage figures: the 2020 Census count for blocks with at least one resident. For all of Puerto Rico it is 3,285,874 people.
definition: The field pop in each municipality record of operators.json coverage: the sum of the 2020 Census residents (the Census field POP100, total people counted in the block) of the municipality's census blocks that have residents. The 78 values add up to 3,285,874, the Puerto Rico total in population_blocks.json.

coverage.frequency: 2020 Census population; recomputed whenever the stops change

method: network.coverage adds block residents by the first five digits of the block code (the county, which is the municipality).
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0
how_to_read: Use it as the denominator for the share of residents near a stop.
caveats: These are 2020 Census counts, not current estimates. The Census Bureau applies privacy protection to block counts, which can shift small blocks.
Census Bureau data are a US Government work; the Bureau asks to be cited as the source.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: summary figures

name: Residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop (coverage records in the operators file)
plain: How many residents live in blocks within 400 metres (about a quarter mile, in a straight line) of a scheduled stop. Using 2020 Census counts and the stops of the 2026-10-02 build, it is 925,788 of 3,285,874 residents in Puerto Rico: 28.2% counting every scheduled stop, 22.2% counting only operators whose timetable has not ended.
definition: Fields served and served_pct in each municipality record of operators.json coverage. served: residents of census blocks whose nearest scheduled stop (any operator, any feed status) is 400 m or less away in a straight line. served_pct: served divided by pop, times 100, one decimal. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 40 of 78 municipalities have 0 residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop. The same values are copied into municipalities.json as pop_served_400m and pop_served_pct.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02); residents are 2020 Census counts

method: network.coverage finds the nearest scheduled stop of each block and keeps the block if the distance is 400 m or less. The block's position is the Census Bureau's internal point. 400 m is about a quarter mile. It is the walking distance the observatory uses, a planning convention and not a legal or engineering standard.
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0; distances use the scheduled stops in transport.json (sources ati_gtfs and muni_gtfs)
how_to_read: A higher share means more residents have a scheduled stop close by. It says nothing about how often vehicles come or where they go. People: 2020 Census. Stops and timetables: build of 2026-10-02.
caveats: Straight-line distance, not walking distance. Hills, rivers, highways and walls can make the real walk longer.
Only scheduled stops count. Stops mapped only in OpenStreetMap are not used.
Stops of expired timetables still count here. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the active figures leave them out: 729,507 residents (22.2%).
A block is counted at one point, so a block that straddles the 400 m line is all in or all out.

If you recompute this from the published block and stop files, the total differs by under 0.1% in the 2026-10 snapshot. Block positions in the file are rounded, and the observatory finds the nearest stop in degrees rather than metres.

A low or zero share can mean that the observatory found no timetable, not that no service runs. In the 2026-10 snapshot, no timetable feed was found in the registry the observatory reads for 15 municipal systems and the públicos authority, and públicos are never counted. Do not rank municipalities by this share without checking each operator's feed status.
Census Bureau data are a US Government work; the Bureau asks to be cited as the source. The stop data carry the terms described in the entry on transit routes.

name: Residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop, excluding expired timetables
plain: Like the 400 m measure, but it leaves out stops of operators whose timetable had ended. With 2020 Census counts and the stops of the 2026-10-02 build, it is 729,507 residents (22.2%) in Puerto Rico, compared with 28.2% when every stop counts.
definition: Fields served_active and served_active_pct in each municipality record of operators.json coverage. served_active: residents of blocks with at least one scheduled stop within 400 m that belongs to an operator whose feed status was not expired on the build date. served_active_pct: that number divided by pop, times 100, one decimal. Copied into municipalities.json as pop_served_active_pct.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02); residents are 2020 Census counts

method: network.coverage queries all scheduled stops within 400 m of each block and skips those whose operator id is in the set of expired operators (inactive_ops).
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0; distances use the scheduled stops in transport.json (sources ati_gtfs and muni_gtfs)
how_to_read: Compare with the all-stops measure. The map calls this a stop with a current timetable; for tourism places the matching measure is municipalities.acc_cur400_pct. The gap shows how much of the measured access depends on timetables that have ended. People: 2020 Census. Stops and timetables: build of 2026-10-02. For example, in the 2026-10-02 build Ponce shows 56.6% with every stop and 0.0% with only active timetables, because its feed ended on 2024-12-31.
caveats: The expired set is fixed on the build date. On 2026-10-02 it includes the 7 operators with an expired feed: Caguas, Cidra, Fajardo, Hatillo, Juncos, Ponce, San Lorenzo. An expiring feed still counts as active.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, in Manatí and Carolina this figure is higher than the all-stops figure (by 35 and 223 residents), because the two are found with different search steps.

A low or zero share can mean that the observatory found no timetable, not that no service runs. In the 2026-10 snapshot, no timetable feed was found in the registry the observatory reads for 15 municipal systems and the públicos authority, and públicos are never counted. Do not rank municipalities by this share without checking each operator's feed status.
