name: Residents within 400 m of Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) stops, municipal stops, or both
plain: How many residents live within 400 metres of a stop of Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), of a municipal system, or of both. With 2020 Census counts and the stops of the 2026-10-02 build, 487,026 residents of Puerto Rico are near an ATI stop, 609,383 are near a municipal stop and 171,389 are near both.
definition: Fields served_ati, served_muni and served_both in each municipality record of operators.json coverage. served_ati: residents of blocks with at least one ATI stop within 400 m. served_muni: residents with at least one stop of a municipal operator (any scheduled stop that is not ATI's) within 400 m. served_both: residents with both. Copied into municipalities.json as pop_served_ati and pop_served_muni.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02); residents are 2020 Census counts

method: network.coverage flags each block for ATI, municipal or both from the stops found within 400 m. Expired municipal feeds still count here.
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0; distances use the scheduled stops in transport.json (sources ati_gtfs and muni_gtfs)
how_to_read: served_both shows where the two kinds of system overlap, which is where coordination matters. People: 2020 Census. Stops and timetables: build of 2026-10-02.
caveats: Expired municipal timetables are included. See the active measure for the version without them.
A resident near a stop of both counts once in served_both and also in served_ati and in served_muni, so the three do not add up.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, in 11 municipalities the all-stops figure differs from served_ati + served_muni - served_both, by up to 287 residents, because the two are found with different search steps.

A low or zero share can mean that the observatory found no timetable, not that no service runs. In the 2026-10 snapshot, no timetable feed was found in the registry the observatory reads for 15 municipal systems and the públicos authority, and públicos are never counted. Do not rank municipalities by this share without checking each operator's feed status.

name: Population by census block, with distance to the nearest scheduled stop
plain: A list of the 36,570 census blocks that had residents in the 2020 Census. Each row gives the block's position, its 2020 population and how far it is from the nearest scheduled stop.
definition: The file population_blocks.json is a list of 36,570 rows, one for each 2020 Census block that has residents. Each row is [longitude, latitude, residents, metres], described under Codes. The rows hold 3,285,874 residents in total (2020 Census). The 2D map uses the file for service gaps and the route planner, and the 3D view uses it for the route planner. The coverage figures in operators.json are computed from the same blocks.

coverage.frequency: 2020 population; the distance column is rewritten whenever the stops change

method: load_blocks in network.py reads the 2020 Census block layer of TIGERweb for Puerto Rico (state code 72), keeps blocks with POP100 above 0 and stores the internal point. coverage() then replaces the block's county code with the distance to the nearest scheduled stop.
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0; distances use the scheduled stops in transport.json (sources ati_gtfs and muni_gtfs)
how_to_read: Add up residents for blocks that meet a distance rule. For example, blocks with metres of 400 or less hold the residents counted as near a stop.
caveats: The 2020 Census applies privacy protection to block counts, so small blocks are not exact.
Positions are rounded, and the distance is a straight line from the block's internal point, not from where people live in the block.

A row is a statistical block with its internal point, not a home. In the 2020 Census counts used, 50 rows hold exactly one resident. Do not use rows with very small counts to identify or locate any household.
Census Bureau data are a US Government work; the Bureau asks to be cited as the source.

values.1st value: longitude: Longitude of the block's internal point, in decimal degrees, rounded to 4 decimals (about 11 m). The internal point is a point the Census Bureau places inside the block, usually near its centre.
values.2nd value: latitude: Latitude of the block's internal point, in decimal degrees, rounded to 4 decimals.
values.3rd value: residents: The 2020 Census population of the block (the Census field POP100, total people counted in the block). Blocks with 0 residents are left out.
values.4th value: metres: Straight-line distance in whole metres from the internal point to the nearest scheduled stop, capped at 9,999. Stops of expired timetables count. It is a distance, not a count of housing units.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Residents far from service

name: Distance from a census block to the nearest scheduled stop
plain: How many metres in a straight line from the block to the closest scheduled stop. Values above 9,999 are shown as 9,999.
definition: The fourth value of each row in population_blocks.json, in whole metres (the decimals are cut off). It uses every scheduled stop in the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal feeds, whatever the state of the feed. In the build of 2026-10-02, values run from 2 to 9999; 6,419 blocks are capped at 9999; and 925,788 residents (28.2%) are in blocks at 400 m or less.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.coverage uses a spatial index to find the nearest stop and converts the degree difference to metres (111,320 m per degree of latitude, shortened for longitude).
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0; distances use the scheduled stops in transport.json (sources ati_gtfs and muni_gtfs)
how_to_read: A small value means a stop is near. Use 400 m for the walk-access measure and 800 m for the service-gap layer.
caveats: The nearest stop is found in degrees, so a few blocks can have a slightly longer distance than the true nearest stop; recomputing the figures from the published files changes the total near 400 m by under 0.1% in the 2026-10 snapshot.
The distance ignores streets, barriers and the timetable. A stop of an expired timetable counts as a stop.
The distance counts stops of expired timetables. For tourism places, the matching distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable is ts_m in place_access.json.

name: Residents far from service (map layer)
plain: Residents who live more than 800 m, in a straight line, from any scheduled stop. The map layer draws a circle for each census block with 40 or more residents that is more than 800 m from a stop. Using 2020 Census counts and the stops of the 2026-10-02 build, 1,986,126 residents (60%) in Puerto Rico live more than 800 m from any stop in a published timetable; the total counts every block, including small ones.
definition: A map layer drawn from population_blocks.json: one circle for each block with more than 800 m to the nearest scheduled stop and at least 40 residents (12,790 blocks in the 2026-10 snapshot). Circle size follows the number of residents. The note on the map counts all residents in blocks more than 800 m from a stop, including blocks with fewer than 40 people.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02); residents are 2020 Census counts

method: The layer filters the rows of population_blocks.json in the browser (network.js, setGaps). 800 m is about half a mile. It is a planning convention chosen by the observatory, not a legal or engineering standard.
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census Blocks (tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10), STATE=72, fields GEOID, POP100, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON, blocks with POP100 above 0; distances use the scheduled stops in transport.json (sources ati_gtfs and muni_gtfs)
how_to_read: Large circles in low-service areas show many residents far from a scheduled stop. People: 2020 Census. Stops and timetables: build of 2026-10-02.
caveats: Stops from expired timetables still count as stops. Públicos, systems for which no timetable feed was found and stops mapped only in OpenStreetMap are not counted. The true gap could therefore be larger or smaller.
Straight-line distance and 2020 counts. It is a planning aid, not a demand forecast.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Residents far from service

name: Integration points: nearby stops of different operators
plain: Places where a stop of one transit system lies within 250 metres of a stop of another system, a starting point for looking at possible transfers. There are 366 in the 2026-10 snapshot.
definition: The transfers list in operators.json has one record for each pair of nearby stops of different operators; its keys are listed under Codes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the total found is 366 (transfers_total) and the list is cut at 600, so all are present. Most pairs involve Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI): 362 of 366.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: network.transfers compares every scheduled stop with the others within 250 m, keeps pairs from different operators, keeps only one pair for each pair of operators in each 0.001-degree cell (about 110 m) around the first stop, and sorts by distance.
how_to_read: A short distance means stops of two systems are almost the same place.
caveats: A pair shows that the stops are close. It does not show that riders can transfer: the observatory does not compare timetables, walking routes or fares.
Stops of expired timetables are included; in the 2026-10 snapshot some pairs involve Caguas, Juncos or San Lorenzo, whose feeds had ended.

values.a: Operator id of the first stop (for example ati).
values.b: Operator id of the second stop.
values.lat: Latitude of the midpoint of the two stops (5 decimals).
values.lng: Longitude of the midpoint of the two stops (5 decimals).
values.d: Distance between the two stops in whole metres (0 to 249 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Integration points

name: Distances used for walking, gaps, transfers and removing duplicates
plain: The observatory uses fixed straight-line distances. 400 m is a walk to a stop, 800 m is a service gap and 250 m is an integration point. Distances from 30 m to 2 km remove duplicate points.
definition: 400 m: about a quarter mile, used for the walk rings on the map, the shares of tourism places near any mapped stop and near a stop with a current timetable, and the resident coverage. 800 m: a service gap, and the outer limit of the 'Stop 400–800 m away' and 'Only expired or unscheduled stops within 800 m' classes of the access profile. 250 m: two stops of different operators count as an integration point. 30 m: an OpenStreetMap (OSM) stop that close to a scheduled stop is treated as the same stop. 200 m (rail stations and ferry terminals) and 100 m (bus stations): OSM station points that close to a same-kind point are folded together. 2 km: an OSM aerodrome that close to a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airport is dropped. 500 m: how far a stop may be moved to reach a road when a route line is snapped.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the program code

method: Constants in network.py (WALK_M, TRANSFER_M), transport.py (WALK_M, HUB_FOLD_M) and access.py (NEAR_M, FAR_M). Distances are computed on a flat approximation: 111,320 m per degree of latitude, and the same figure scaled by the cosine of the latitude for longitude.
how_to_read: All distances are straight lines, not walking routes.
caveats: The distances are planning conventions chosen for the observatory, not legal or engineering standards.

name: Typical weekday, Saturday and Sunday service
plain: Weekday trip counts show one reference day, usually Wednesday, so trips that run only on other weekdays are not included. Saturday and Sunday use their own timetables. Holidays are not modelled.
definition: The reference weekday is Wednesday, or the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that the feed actually serves. A trip counts as weekday service if its service pattern runs on that day, as Saturday service if its pattern runs on Saturday and as Sunday service if it runs on Sunday. A pattern that runs on several day types counts in each. If a trip names a service that the feed does not define, it counts as weekday service. If a feed has no calendar.txt, every service listed in calendar_dates.txt counts as running on every day type.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: parse_gtfs in network.py. The feed's start and end dates for each pattern are not checked, and exceptions in calendar_dates.txt (holidays, added or removed dates) are not applied when the feed has a calendar.txt.
how_to_read: Read weekday counts as the number of trips on a normal Wednesday, not an average of the week.
caveats: The Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed read on 2026-10-02 has a pattern named Holiday_Service_Route_1. Its calendar covers every Monday to Friday from 2026-07-27 to 2027-05-31, but for its Monday and Wednesday pattern the feed's exceptions file removes 87 dates and adds 6. The observatory does not apply exceptions, so the 30 trips of that pattern count as ordinary weekday trips on route 1: 81 in the file, 51 without them.
Service on public holidays, school breaks or special events is not modelled.
A feed whose patterns cover different date ranges is counted as if all ran together.

name: Timetable replay files: weekday, Saturday and Sunday trips
plain: Three files that hold every scheduled trip as its stops and times along its route's line, so the map and the 3D view can show vehicles on their timetable, following the roads. They are not Global Positioning System (GPS) data.
definition: A trip is one scheduled run of a vehicle along a route, as listed in a feed (the set of GTFS files in which an operator publishes its stops, routes, trips and times). In the 2026-10 snapshot, trips.json (weekday, typical Wednesday service) holds 3,297 trips from 25 operators. trips_sa.json (Saturday) holds 1,648 trips from 4 operators: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), Guaynabo, Juncos and Vega Alta. trips_su.json (Sunday) holds 381 trips from 1 operator, ATI. Each file has five keys: day (a label, which reads 'weekday (typical Wednesday service)' in trips.json, 'Saturday' in trips_sa.json and 'Sunday' in trips_su.json); format (2); paths (one path for each stop pattern, that is each set of trips that stop at the same places in the same order: a list of [longitude, latitude, metres from the start of the path] along the route's line, at 5 decimals); path_kind (for each path, 'line' when it follows the route's line, or 'stops' when no line fits the stops and the path joins them in straight lines); and trips (the list; see Trip record). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 3,297 weekday trips share 222 stop patterns, 206 of them along their route's line. Only trips with at least two stop times are kept. Trips of the five Patillas routes with an inferred stop order are left out: in the 2026-10 snapshot the operator trips_weekday values in operators.json add up to 3,312, while trips.json holds 3,297 (15 Patillas trips left out). Trips of expired and expiring operators remain in the files: in the 2026-10 snapshot, 372 weekday trips belong to expired operators.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: parse_gtfs in network.py reads each trip's stops and times. trip_paths.py places the stops of each trip on one line of its route (the operator's own shape, or the road network that network.py snaps the route to), in travel order, and keeps the part of the line between the first and the last stop, simplified to about 5 m. Trips with the same stops in the same order share one path. refresh_network.py and build.py save the files. The 2D map loads the file that matches today's day in Puerto Rico; the 3D view loads the weekday file. Between two stops, a vehicle's time is spread along the path in proportion to distance (tripPoints in common.js).
how_to_read: Each trip is one scheduled run, drawn along its route's line. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 3,191 of the 3,297 weekday trips follow their route line; the other 106 (16 stop patterns whose stops do not fit any line of their route) join their stops in straight lines and are marked 'stops' in path_kind. Speeds between stops come from the timetable, so a vehicle keeps its scheduled times but moves at an even speed between two stops. A timetable covers the dates from the operator's feed.start to feed.end in operators.json, not the build date. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31; Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31. Cite both the build date and the feed dates.
caveats: The files hold timetables, not observed positions.
The 3D view replays every weekday trip in trips.json, including those of expired timetables; the 2D map leaves expired operators out.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, two weekday trips of Ponce (route Tuque) have one stop time that is far earlier than the stops around it, so the replay would place the vehicle oddly. Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31, so the 2D map skips these trips; the 3D view does not.

Terms differ by source. The terms of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) say the data are provided as is, without warranty, and that an app built on them must make clear it is not affiliated with or sponsored by ATI. The municipal feeds state no license; ask the municipality before reusing a feed beyond viewing it. Parts drawn from OpenStreetMap are under the Open Database License (credit and share-alike). Check each source's terms before reuse.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Vehicles on their timetable now
3D view: Day clock with the replay of weekday transit

name: Trip record: route, mode, operator, stop pattern and stop times
plain: One scheduled trip. It has the route label, the mode, the operator, the path it follows along its route, where its stops are on that path, and the time at each stop.
definition: Each trip (one scheduled run of a vehicle along a route, as listed in a feed) is an object with six keys. r: the route label (the route's short name, or its long name if there is no short name). m: the mode. o: the operator id. k: the trip's path, an index into the file's paths (the stop pattern it shares with every trip that stops at the same places in the same order). s: for each stop time, the index of the point of that path where the stop is. t: the time at each stop, in seconds after midnight, in stop order. A stop time is a line in the feed saying that the trip calls at a stop at a given time; the time is the departure time at the stop, or the arrival time if there is no departure time. Times are local; General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) allows times after 24:00 for trips that run past midnight, but in the 2026-10 snapshot no time in these files is above 86,400 (24:00). In the same snapshot, one Saturday trip and one Sunday trip, both Tren Urbano (TU), end exactly at 86,400; no weekday trip does (the latest weekday time is 86,340, 23:59). The weekday file has 78,414 stop times in that snapshot. A stop sits on its path a median 7 m from the stop's own coordinates (95% within 13 m), because the path follows the road line.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and the files are rewritten only when a feed changes. Snapshot built 2026-10-02.

method: Built in parse_gtfs (network.py) from the feed's stop_times.txt; trip_paths.py fits the stops to the route line and writes k, s and t. To get the vehicle's position at any time, walk the path between two stops and spread the time between them by distance (tripPoints in site/js/common.js does this).
how_to_read: The value list shows the codes of m. The route label r can be matched with the short or long name of a route of the same operator. The stop times t are the timetable itself: use them, not the path points, to count departures, measure headways or find transfers. Trips that share k are one service pattern of a route, which is the unit to compare supply between routes.
caveats: A route label is only unique within one operator.
A trip with a gap in its stop times only has the stops that carry times, so its path can skip stops.

name: Vehicles on their timetable now (timetable replay)
plain: A map layer that shows where each scheduled vehicle should be right now, in Puerto Rico time, according to the published timetable. It is not live Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking and does not show real vehicle positions.
definition: For the current Puerto Rico day, the map picks the Sunday, Saturday or weekday file. A trip counts as in service when the current time is between its first and last stop time. Its position is worked out in a straight line between the two stops that surround the current time, in proportion to the time elapsed. The layer refreshes every 5 seconds and shows the total and the largest operators.

coverage.frequency: Recalculated every 5 seconds in your browser while the layer is on, from timetable files rewritten when a feed changes (last write: 2026-10-02)

method: updateNow in network.js. Trips of operators whose feed is expired on today's date are skipped. Holidays are not modelled.
how_to_read: Read it as where the schedule says vehicles are, not where they are. The number is worked out in your browser every 5 seconds and is not stored in any file. To cite it, give the date, the Puerto Rico clock time shown in the layer note, the build date of the timetables and the feed dates. A timetable covers the dates from the operator's feed.start to feed.end in operators.json, not the build date. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31; Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31.
caveats: Real-time bus positions do not exist in the data; see Real-time data.
The position is a straight line between stops, so a vehicle can appear off the road.
A late or cancelled vehicle is shown as on time. On a Monday or Friday the weekday file still shows the reference weekday's timetable, usually Wednesday's.
Only operators with a published timetable appear. Operators with no feed, públicos and OpenStreetMap routes are absent.

Each marker is one scheduled trip in progress, not an identified vehicle: the trip files hold no vehicle ids. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on Saturday only 4 operators, and on Sunday only ATI, have timetable files, so a lower weekend count does not show how much service runs.
